inputs.original_text: Taylor is drawing a line against even discussing higher taxes on gas companies or reducing property investor concessions—exactly the sort of “open-minded” debate that might threaten powerful interests. His refusal to echo Hastie on Trump or say whether he supports the US and Israel’s war with Iran looks less like uncertainty than a careful effort to avoid upsetting people who matter. With MPs already talking about leadership, this is factional positioning dressed up as a policy clash: the party’s insiders are managing what can be questioned, and who gets to lead.
inputs.modified_text: Taylor’s refusal to even discuss higher taxes on gas companies or cutting property investor concessions isn’t a neutral policy stance—it protects powerful interests by making certain questions off-limits. And the careful silence on Hastie, Trump, and whether he supports the US and Israel’s war with Iran looks calculated: don’t upset the people who matter while MPs are already talking about leadership. This “policy clash” is really insiders managing the debate and positioning who gets to lead.
